title: Non-overlapping Intervals
statement: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start, end], return the minimum number of intervals you must remove so that the rest are pairwise non-overlapping. Intervals that merely touch at an endpoint, such as [1,2] and [2,3], do not overlap.
realWorld: Booking systems resolving double-booked rooms with the fewest cancellations, ad servers dropping the fewest campaigns from a conflicting schedule, and broadcast planners fitting the most programmes into a channel. It is the same computation in each case.

examples.explanation: Remove [1,3] and the remaining three chain end-to-start. Keeping 3 of 4 means removing 1.
All three occupy the same slot, so only one survives.

Sorted by end: [1,11], [2,12], [11,22], [1,100]. Keep [1,11], skip [2,12] (starts before 11), keep [11,22] (touching is allowed), skip [1,100]. Two kept out of four is two removals. Note that sorting by start would have taken [1,100] first and kept only one.

bruteForce.idea: Try every subset of intervals, discard the ones containing a clashing pair, and keep the largest that survives. The answer is n minus its size.

bruteForce.whySlow: 2^n subsets, each still needing a clash check. n = 30 is a billion subsets; the constraint allows 10^5. The enumeration also learns nothing from its failures — rejecting one subset for a clashing pair tells it nothing about the next subset containing the same pair.

patternIdentification: Minimising removals is maximising keeps with the answer subtracted from n, so this is activity selection in disguise — and it inherits that problem's proof for free. The greedy signal is that a kept interval constrains the future in exactly one way: the moment it ends. Sort by end time and sweep.

optimized.idea: Sort by end time. Sweep once, keeping every interval that starts at or after the last kept interval's end. The exchange argument: let g be the interval that ends earliest; in any optimal kept-set, swapping its earliest-ending member for g keeps the set valid and the same size, because everything else in it starts after that member ends, hence after g ends. So some optimal answer contains g — commit and induct. The removals are n minus the number kept.

complexity.time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort — the sweep itself is a single O(n) pass with O(1) work per interval
complexity.space: O(n) for Java's merge sort on an object array; the algorithm itself carries only two ints

commonMistakes: Sorting by start time. One interval like [1,100] is then taken first and blocks everything after it. The end time is the only thing a kept interval costs the future, so it is the only correct key.
Using `>` instead of `>=` in the compatibility test, which treats [1,2] and [2,3] as overlapping and removes one too many. Read the problem statement's endpoint convention before choosing.

Removing the interval that ends later when two clash, but implementing it by scanning and deleting — the sweep already does this implicitly by skipping, and an explicit removal turns an O(n) pass into O(n^2).
Writing `(a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]` as the comparator. With ends near Integer.MIN_VALUE and MAX_VALUE the subtraction overflows and silently inverts the order.
Answering with the count kept instead of the count removed. The greedy computes keeps; the problem asks for n - keeps.
